category.title: Number Theory & Prime Mathematics
category.description: Fundamental and advanced competitive programming number theory algorithms: Primality testing, Factorization, Euclidean & Extended Euclidean, Sieve of Eratosthenes, Segmented Sieve, and Linear Sieve (SPF).

algorithms.title: Primality Testing & Factor Extraction (Divisibility)
algorithms.summary: Check if a number is Prime or Composite and extract all unique factors/divisors in O(sqrt(N)) time.
explanation: 1. Divisibility Property: If `N = a * b`, at least one factor must be `<= sqrt(N)`.
2. Primality Test: Loop `d` from 2 to `sqrt(N)`. If `N % d == 0`, N is composite.
3. Factor Extraction: Iterate `d` from 1 to `sqrt(N)`. If `d` divides N, add `d` and paired factor `N / d` to factors list.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Primality and Factors of N = 36

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Checks prime status and enumerates all divisors of an integer in O(sqrt(N)) time.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When verifying individual numbers for primality or finding all factors.
wAnswers.whereUsed: RSA cryptography key validation, modular math factorizations.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(sqrt(N)) replaces naive O(N) trial division.

algorithms.title: Euclidean Algorithm (GCD & LCM)
algorithms.summary: Computes Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) using Euclidean division algorithm and Least Common Multiple (LCM) via formula LCM(A, B) = (A * B) / GCD(A, B).
explanation: 1. Euclidean Reduction: `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b)`.
2. Base Case: When `b == 0`, `gcd(a, 0) = a`.
3. LCM Relation: `LCM(a, b) * GCD(a, b) = a * b`, so `LCM(a, b) = (a * b) // GCD(a, b)`.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Calculates highest common factor and lowest common multiple in O(log N) operations.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When simplifying fractions, computing periodic cycles, or reducing modular equations.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Fraction arithmetic reduction, clock synchronization, competitive programming math.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Logarithmic reduction `O(log(min(A, B)))` by repeatedly taking remainder.

algorithms.title: Extended Euclidean Algorithm (Modular Inverse)
algorithms.summary: Solves linear Diophantine equation `a*x + b*y = gcd(a, b)` and calculates modular multiplicative inverse `(a * x) % m = 1`.
explanation: 1. Bézout's Identity: For non-zero integers `a` and `b`, integers `x` and `y` exist such that `a*x + b*y = gcd(a, b)`.
2. Extended Euclidean Recurrence: `gcd, x1, y1 = extGCD(b, a % b)`, then `x = y1` and `y = x1 - (a // b) * y1`.
3. Modular Multiplicative Inverse: If `gcd(a, m) == 1`, `(a * x) % m = 1`. `x % m` gives the modular inverse of `a` modulo `m`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Extended GCD(30, 20)
traceSteps: Recursive call extGCD(10, 0) -> Returns (gcd=10, x=1, y=0)

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes Bézout coefficients and modular multiplicative inverse in O(log N) time.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When finding modular inverses for combination counting modulo 10^9+7 or solving Diophantine equations.
wAnswers.whereUsed: RSA public key encryption, modular division in combinatorics, Chinese Remainder Theorem.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Logarithmic complexity O(log N) for modular inverse calculation.

algorithms.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes (Primes up to N)
algorithms.summary: Precomputes prime status for all numbers up to N in near-linear O(N log log N) time.
explanation: 1. Create boolean array `is_prime[0..N]` initialized to True. Set `is_prime[0] = is_prime[1] = False`.
2. Iterate `p` from 2 to `sqrt(N)`. If `is_prime[p]` is True, mark all multiples of `p` starting from `p*p` as False.
3. All remaining True entries represent prime numbers.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Generates all prime numbers up to N in near-linear time.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When checking multiple prime queries or needing prime table up to N=10^7.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Competitive programming prime precomputation, prime factor counting.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(N log log N) is practically linear for N = 10^7.

algorithms.title: Segmented Sieve (Primes in Range [L, R])
algorithms.summary: Generates all prime numbers in range [L, R] where R can be up to 10^12 and segment length R - L <= 10^6.
explanation: 1. Generate base primes up to `sqrt(R)` using standard Sieve of Eratosthenes.
2. Create boolean array `dummy[0..R-L]` initialized to True for interval `[L, R]`.
3. For each base prime `p`, find smallest multiple `first_multiple >= L`. Mark multiples `first_multiple` through `R` as False in `dummy` array.
4. Avoids allocated O(R) memory array, allowing prime generation for huge numbers up to 10^12.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Segmented Sieve for L=10, R=20
traceSteps: Base primes up to sqrt(20) = 4 -> Primes: [2, 3].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Generates primes in a large range [L, R] without storing huge arrays in memory.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When range endpoints R are large (up to 10^12) but query interval length R - L is small (<= 10^6).
wAnswers.whereUsed: Competitive programming large range prime counting problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(R - L + 1) memory footprint instead of allocating O(R) array.

algorithms.title: Linear Sieve (Euler's Sieve & Smallest Prime Factor - SPF)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N) Sieve, O(log N) Factorization Query
algorithms.summary: Strictly O(N) linear time prime sieve that also records Smallest Prime Factor (SPF) for instant O(log N) prime factorization queries.
explanation: 1. Single Composite Marking: Every composite number is marked EXACTLY ONCE by its smallest prime factor.
2. SPF Array: `spf[i]` stores smallest prime factor dividing `i`.
3. Linear Loop: For each number `i`, iterate through discovered `primes`. Mark `i * p` composite with `spf[i * p] = p`. STOP loop when `i % p == 0`.
4. O(log N) Factorization Query: Repeatedly divide `N` by `spf[N]` until `N == 1`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace SPF Factorization of N = 60
traceSteps: Precomputed SPF array up to N=60.
Prime Factors of 60: [2, 2, 3, 5] in O(log N) time!

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Generates primes in strictly linear O(N) time and performs O(log N) factorizations for Q queries.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When answering thousands of prime factorization queries in competitive programming.
wAnswers.whereUsed: High performance competitive programming factorization, multiplicative functions precomputation.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Strict O(N) linear time without redundant multiple composite markings.
